name: Uma Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an aluminium-tube extrusion machine on nights, checking the first tube wall after each die change. I came from a uniform factory and am still a junior learning this line at fifty-eight, with secondary-school education. Night premiums lift my pay above the usual operator rate, but the senior setter checks my first run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mae delivers books for a library service, and our grown children have homes of their own. We have a housing loan, almost a year of expenses saved and plenty of nearby metal plants. I use AI daily to group thickness alarms, then measure the actual tube before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tube crew that a little AI help is still worth using if it catches a bad wall thickness early. I would keep measuring the first aluminium tube after each die change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am fifty-eight and new to extrusion after years at a uniform factory, so the senior setter still checks my first run. Night premiums give me better-than-usual operator pay, and Mae and I have nearly a year saved with our grown children living elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid night shift, record the micrometer readings and use my existing AI log every day to group faulty runs. From each full wage month I would add a fresh amount to savings after our housing payment and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm about the job. A steady factory month gives us time to ask what retirement might actually cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake have you made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once set the die a little too wide and the tube wall was thin. The setter caught the first piece, and I keep that sample beside my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does AI do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It groups thickness alarms and suggests which die to inspect. I still measure the metal and check the paper setup card before stopping a run.

say: I would welcome **small thickness warnings** from AI when they help me stop a bad extrusion run.
I would keep **first-tube measurements** after die changes.
think: My **night premium** lifts this junior wage above the usual rate for an operator.
Our **year-long reserve** and nearby metal plants provide choices.
do: Keep **paid night shifts** and micrometer checks.
Use the **existing daily AI log** for faults.
Save fresh **full-month wages** after housing and food.
feel: **Calm** about current work and household money.
S0.quote: The setter caught the first piece, and I keep that sample beside my notebook.
fieldNote: Uma’s **late move to extrusion** keeps her junior despite years of factory work.
Her **strong reserve** support calm; additional savings come from current paid wages.

steps.text: Keep night extrusion shifts and measure first tubes
Save fresh full-month wages after housing and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask management for the error rate and the paid roster together before expanding camera checks. Software may change ordering quickly; robot die handling needs a slower safe test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera could take the simple thickness checks I am still learning. I use AI daily and could learn a new station, but being a junior on nights means my own hours could be cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an offered paid guarded trial on twenty sample tubes with the senior setter present. If approved, I would learn the new AI camera threshold on test metal and compare it with my micrometer; after an actual shift cut, I would apply for posted reachable extrusion work only if net pay after travel covers our housing costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own rota, even with savings. A reserve is a bridge to another paid shift, not a reason to accept a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you just run the new camera now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The setter would need to isolate the reject gate and give me a paid practice slot. I have asked for that, not been offered it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you raise with the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roster beside the camera error figures. I would ask the branch to insist on posted transfer jobs before anyone loses a night shift.

say: I would demand **errors and paid hours** on the same sheet.
I would separate **ordering software** from robot die work.
think: A camera could remove **my junior checks**.
My **night shifts** may be the first cut despite a strong reserve.
do: Request **twenty-tube guarded test** only with offered paid practice.
Learn **new AI thresholds** on approved test metal.
Apply after **shift cuts** only for posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible loss of her own paid week.
S1.quote: A reserve is a bridge to another paid shift, not a reason to accept a bad one.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** makes new camera learning plausible, while her junior status keeps hours at risk.
The trial needs an **offered paid safe place**; job moves require actual cuts and adequate local pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the night crew that thinking AGI might arrive in 2028 when I am sixty, while capable hands-on robots reach extrusion around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Planning changes first; die work follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the camera and robots could remove my junior shift when they handle dies and reject thin tubes without people. Mae’s library-delivery wage and our near-year reserve buy time, but I do not know which of the nearby plants would still be hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the planned car upgrade and ask for written staffing dates. If my hours end, I would apply for posted reachable metal work only where net pay after travel covers our housing and bills; if no adequate opening appears, I would ask the lender about temporary payment terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, with real risk but a search I can make. I would not call an empty vacancy board a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need actual pension and housing figures before leaving a paid shift. A year saved is helpful, but it is not lifetime income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mae work more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would check the delivery rota first. I would not count unoffered hours as money the household already has.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would seek **written staffing dates** before cuts.
think: My **junior extrusion shift** could go when robots change dies.
A **year saved** buys search time but no guaranteed local vacancy.
do: Stop **car-upgrade plans** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable metal work at bill-covering net pay.
Ask **lender** about temporary terms if no adequate role appears.
feel: **Anxious** about job risk, with savings and local options to test.
S2.quote: I would not call an empty vacancy board a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Physical robots arrive around **age sixty-three**, after the thinking-AI change.
Her **reserve and nearby plants** support a search; applications and lender relief remain conditional on real offers and approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three and capable robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is enough for the plant to pay for real practical places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into measurement and quality work if a local plant posts a role. I am still learning extrusion, so I would need supervised practice and a recognised qualification before claiming I can sign off parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid night shift and put fresh surplus from full months against our housing loan. If the plant offers a funded paid-time quality course with an isolated measurement place and a posted reachable job at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying, I would apply for that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to compare a real course with our bills. A certificate without supervised parts and a wage is just paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified inspector would stop the line and let me measure wall thickness across a sample batch. I would need an offered paid place and signed feedback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no quality job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep extrusion shifts and compare nearby posted machine jobs if hours fall. The housing loan still needs paid work, so I would not enrol on hope.

say: I would demand **paid practical places** before 2034 robots.
I would use **posted quality wages** to judge a course.
think: My **junior extrusion skill** needs a recognised qualification before I can sign off quality checks.
The **housing loan** still needs income at sixty-six.
do: Keep **night shifts** and pay extra housing loan from new wages.
Enrol in **funded paid quality training** only with safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to compare real terms.
S3.quote: A certificate without supervised parts and a wage is just paper.
fieldNote: She uses **new technology readily** but still needs recognised inspection practice.
The later **application** requires an offered funded paid safe place, posted reachable role and sufficient net wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. A decade gives workers time to check retirement income and real posts, if employers publish them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mae and I would like to stop full-time work before seventy-one, but I cannot promise the housing loan is gone or a pension covers our bills. Our grown children have their own households and should not become our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the extrusion shift and pay a fresh extra amount against our housing loan from full wages. I would request retirement figures with Mae; in the first year after 2036, if still employed because we need income, I would check actual rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for posted reachable safe work at bill-covering net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant robots while we have wages and a strong reserve now. I want a number on the retirement sheet that covers the housing payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave work before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income, Mae’s confirmed wages and our reserve cover housing, food and repairs. If they fall short, I would keep safe paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach another worker the AI log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already show new starters the daily log, but that is not a new skill for me. I would teach on paid time if the plant asked.

I would keep **2036 thinking AI** separate from 2039 die robots.
think: Our **housing loan** and future pension remain uncertain when the robot date is thirteen years away.
Grown children should not become our **cash reserve**.
do: Keep **2026 extrusion shifts** and pay extra housing loan from wages.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only if employed and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current finances remain sound.
S4.quote: I want a number on the retirement sheet that covers the housing payment.
fieldNote: Her **current 2026 work** is separate from conditional post-2036 employment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable die-handling robots around 2031 could take my junior night shift before our housing loan is cleared. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the first tube is still checked by someone who has seen a thin wall. A neat computer chart cannot hold a pipe together.

headlineQuote: A neat computer chart cannot hold a pipe together.
portrait: **Uma**, 58, is a junior extrusion operator on nights after changing from uniform-factory work, with secondary schooling and developing skill.
Her **library-delivery partner**, grown children, housing loan, higher night pay, near-year reserve and many local metal plants give options.
She uses **AI daily** for fault grouping and would learn camera controls through offered paid guarded testing.
Fast robots threaten **die work** at sixty-three; longer warning permits conditional quality training and verified retirement planning.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could remove her junior extrusion shift around 2031 while the housing loan still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe instruction and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
